query: Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloys have reported densities of 1.46–6 g/cm3 and commonly contain solid solutions together with intermetallic compounds. Earlier induction-melted Al–Mg-rich alloys established this structural complexity but did not resolve subsequent transformation pathways. Compositionally graded MgAlCuZnGd alloys showed region-dependent compression and corrosion performance, while studies of AlMgₓTiSnZn alloys associated Mg content with phase stability and multiple functional properties. Most prior work emphasized hardness and room-temperature compression, leaving corrosion, high-temperature oxidation, and evolution from metastable states comparatively underexplored. Within the design constraint of density below 6 g/cm3 and the tendency for constituent-property differences to promote stable intermetallic compounds, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain how a non-equilibrium Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy evolves and why that evolution changes its corrosion and high-temperature oxidation behavior? Specify an unnamed controlled comparison, predictions relative to the initial baseline, boundary conditions, supporting prior observations, and an outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In non‐equilibrium Mg‐containing lightweight high-entropy alloys, thermal exposure drives Mg to segregate to grain boundaries and intermetallic interfaces, triggering the transformation of a heterogeneous, metastable microstructure into a refined structure with stable intermetallic phases and Mg-enriched regions that form a protective oxide film, thereby improving corrosion resistance and high-temperature oxidation behavior.
generation.material_initial_state: A rapidly solidified, induction-melted Mg-containing lightweight HEA (density <6 g/cm³) exhibiting a metastable mix of a primary solid solution and dispersed intermetallic compounds.
generation.intervention: Application of a controlled thermal exposure (annealing at elevated temperatures representative of service conditions) to initiate microstructural evolution.
generation.conditions: Experiments conducted in air and/or corrosive media at temperatures high enough to activate diffusion (e.g., above 300°C) while maintaining the density and overall alloy composition constraints.
generation.structural_mediator: Mg segregation at grain boundaries and interphase regions that mediates a transformation of unstable intermetallic phases into more stable, passivated forms and promotes the in situ formation of a coherent Mg-rich oxide scale.
generation.mechanism: Upon thermal exposure, Mg diffuses from the metastable matrix to interfaces and grain boundaries. This localized enrichment facilitates the transformation of heterogeneous intermetallic phases into thermodynamically more stable compounds that incorporate Mg. Concurrently, the Mg-enriched regions oxidize to form a protective, adherent oxide film that reduces active corrosion sites and enhances oxidation resistance.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the as-cast baseline, the thermally treated alloy will show a more uniform microstructure with refined stable intermetallic phases, the presence of a coherent Mg-rich oxide/passivation film, a less negative corrosion potential, lower corrosion current densities, and reduced high-temperature oxidation rates.
generation.baseline: The as-cast, rapidly solidified alloy exhibiting a heterogeneous distribution of metastable phases without significant Mg segregation or well-developed protective oxide films.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is predicted to hold for Mg-containing HEAs with densities below 6 g/cm³ and within processing conditions that do not lead to complete homogenization or uncontrolled phase separation; extreme thermal exposures or deviations in composition may produce alternate behaviors.
generation.uncertainty: The precise kinetics of Mg diffusion and the quantitative evolution of phase stability are not fully resolved and may be influenced by complex multi-element interactions; additional detailed studies are required to determine the transformation rates and oxide layer compositions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of Mg-containing lightweight HEA samples (density <6 g/cm³) using identical rapid-melting procedures. Subject one set to controlled thermal annealing (simulating high-temperature service conditions) while leaving the other set as-cast. Subsequently, perform standardized corrosion (potentiodynamic polarization) and high-temperature oxidation tests on both sets.
measurements: Corrosion potential (Ecorr) and corrosion current density (icorr) via electrochemical testing
Weight gain during high-temperature oxidation tests
Microstructural analysis (using SEM/EDS) focusing on Mg segregation, intermetallic phase distribution, and oxide scale formation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the annealed samples do not show statistically significant improvements (i.e., a shift to more noble Ecorr values, reduction in icorr, and evidence of a coherent Mg-rich oxide layer) compared to the as-cast baseline, then the hypothesis that Mg-mediated segregation and phase transformation are responsible for the improved corrosion and oxidation behavior is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: High entropy alloys (HEAs), which include multiple principal elements, have attracted substantial research attention due to their exceptional mechanical properties, such as high fracture toughness, hardness, fatigue and corrosion resistances, yield strength, ductility and thermal stability,,,. In many applications, HEAs can significantly outperform traditional and super-alloys, especially at low and high temperatures,. Recently, the design of lightweight HEAs (with a density lower than 5 g/cc) has become one of the hottest research topics in metallurgy. In view of the outstanding performance of HEAs, the lightweight HEAs may have superior performance than traditional lightweight materials such as Al, Mg, and Ti alloys, with a large number of potential industry applications. Yet the chemical and compositional design space of HEAs is exceptionally vast, which makes the use of the traditional experimental methods for HEA screening an overwhelming task. Thus, an efficient, accurate strategy is required for the design of lightweight HEAs for specific applications,. The aim of the present work is to investigate the influence of systematic variations in Mg content on the microstructure, mechanical properties, and corrosion behavior of these alloys. By characterizing the resulting intermetallic phases, grain refinement, and passive film formation, this study identified how processing and composition synergistically affect the corrosion resistance and mechanical performance. This work offers new insights into the design of corrosion-resistant, high-strength materials and represents a novel extension of compositionally complex alloy design to Mg-rich systems.
